<reason>B better justified and weighed the allocation rule: reciprocity identifies eligible communities, while a lottery prevents wealth from deciding access within that allocation. A raised legitimate concerns about excluded outsiders and imperfect eligibility, but repeatedly treated calling the reservation a privilege as sufficient to defeat its justification. B acknowledged those costs and defended a bounded reservation alongside continued general sale. A’s answer that priced-out members could buy if they valued attendance enough also reinforced B’s distinction between purchasing power and commitment.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>B directly defeated A’s inference that an imperfect poverty or passion test cannot improve access: reciprocity determines eligibility, and the lottery improves poorer eligible applicants’ chances. B also weakened A’s automatic-surcharge claim by noting that reserved-ticket recipients leave general-sale demand as well as inventory.</best_rebuttal>
